text: Did you know that Leonardo Cinami wrote 16 letters to Vitelleschi — more than any other single writer?
Did you know that “the Indies” is the most desired destination in the collection, named in 108 letters?
Did you know that the longest letter in the collection is Letter 3, running to about 1,262 words?
Did you know that the shortest letter is a single sentence? “I, the least of all men, ardently desire to be sent to India.”
Did you know that Francesco Demstero wrote both the shortest letter in the collection — a single sentence — and Letter 100, which was never translated?
Did you know that Letter 100 is missing from the collection? Its database transcription is only placeholder text, so it was never translated.
Did you know that 1640 was the busiest year in the collection, with 25 letters?
Did you know that no letters survive from 1622, 1623, 1645, or 1646?
Did you know that the printed index lists Letter 146 under “Philippines, mission to” — yet the writer himself says he has “no vocation” for the Philippines? His heart was set on Japan.
Did you know that the writer of Letter 79 pointedly refused to name a destination? “I do not pray you to send me to Peru, or to any other country by name.”
Did you know that St. Francis Xavier is invoked in 14 letters — more than any other saint?
Did you know that 132 of the 169 letters are indexed under the theme of “Humility”?
Did you know that the collection opens on January 3, 1616, with Giovanni Battista Astria writing from Genoa?
Did you know that the final letter, dated February 20, 1647, was written from Milan?
Did you know that Letter 119 breaks off mid-sentence? It survives incomplete, ending “(the letter breaks off here).”
Did you know that Marco Stella wrote letters from 4 different places — tied for the most of any writer, with Antonio Rondonio?
Did you know that Japan was the second-most desired destination, named in 33 letters?
Did you know that only one writer in the whole collection asked Vitelleschi for the grace to visit the Holy House of Loreto?
